mcqs.question: What specifically goes wrong at a call site like `new HttpRequest(url, 5000, 3, null)`?
options: It fails to compile because too many arguments were passed
It automatically defaults to the four-argument overload regardless of order
Positional arguments give no indication of which value maps to which parameter, so swapped order compiles but breaks silently
It throws a runtime exception if any argument is null
mcqs.explanation: The compiler only checks types and count, not meaning — if two `int` parameters were swapped, it would still compile and run, just with the wrong values. Nothing here fails to compile, defaults aren't picked automatically based on values, and a null argument doesn't inherently throw.

mcqs.question: When is adding a Director object to a Builder actually worth it?
options: When the exact same sequence of builder calls needs to run from multiple places
Always — every Builder implementation should include one
Only when the product class has no required fields
Never — Director was deprecated in modern object-oriented design
mcqs.explanation: A Director earns its keep by capturing a reusable call sequence so multiple callers don't repeat it. It's not mandatory for every Builder — most fluent builders skip it entirely — and it has nothing to do with whether the product has required fields, nor is it a deprecated concept.

mcqs.question: In the `HttpRequest`/`Builder` code, why is the `HttpRequest` constructor marked private?
options: Private constructors run faster than public ones
It's required syntax whenever a nested Builder class exists
It prevents the Builder class itself from being instantiated
It forces every HttpRequest to be created through the Builder, so build() can't be bypassed
mcqs.explanation: Making the constructor private closes off the one bypass that would let code skip the builder's validation — the only path to an `HttpRequest` is through `build()`. It has no effect on speed, isn't required syntax, and doesn't prevent instantiating `Builder`, which is a separate class.

mcqs.question: A team is choosing between Builder and named parameters in a language like Kotlin, for a class with five optional fields and no cross-field validation needed. What does the comparison suggest?
options: Builder is strictly better in every language, regardless of features
Named parameters solve the readability problem with none of a Builder class's boilerplate, so prefer them here
Constructor overloading is the best fit for exactly five parameters
Builder is required whenever a class has more than three fields
mcqs.explanation: Named parameters give the same readable, self-documenting call site as Builder without an extra class, so when a language has them and there's no multi-field validation to centralize, they're the simpler fit. Builder isn't universally superior — it's solving a problem languages with named parameters don't have — and constructor overloading still has the positional-argument problem regardless of field count.

mcqs.question: A Builder's `build()` method copies whatever fields were set into the product, with no checks, even if none were set. What's the consequence?
options: None — Builder's structure guarantees the product is always valid
The code fails to compile
A half-configured, invalid object can be returned and fail somewhere far from the actual misconfiguration
The builder itself becomes immutable after one use
mcqs.explanation: Builder's structure only produces safety if `build()` enforces it — without validation, an incomplete object slips through and fails later, far from where the missing field was actually set. There's no compile-time guarantee of validity, and nothing about a missing check makes the builder itself immutable.
